blocks.text: The Mirror of Passers-by Between a fleeting moment, voyeurism and a poetic gaze

The street is a river of anonymous figures where solitary souls cross paths without always meeting. We walk amongst them, pass them by, forget them. Yet sometimes just a few seconds are enough for a face, a silhouette or a gesture to be etched into our memory. This is where street photography begins. But looking is never an entirely innocent act. Observing someone without them realising they are being watched, waiting for a gesture, following a silhouette with one’s eyes, lingering on an intimate pose: there is, in the very act of photographing strangers, something that borders on voyeurism. What am I really looking for in other people? An image? An emotion? A story I don’t know? Or simply the pleasure of catching a glimpse of something not meant for me? The gaze that draws near There is a kind of exhilaration in watching strangers go about their lives. Observing without being invited. Guessing a story from a gait, an item of clothing, a demeanour. Imagining what is going on behind a face we will probably never see again. The photographer finds themselves in a strange position: they are watching, whilst the person they are watching is sometimes completely unaware of this attention. This is precisely where unease can arise. The camera gives the gaze an extra power. It allows us to capture what, in everyday life, we would have merely glimpsed. It transforms a fleeting glance into a permanent record. A passer-by who was simply walking past suddenly becomes an image. A gesture that was meant to last only a second is preserved. Something has been captured. But what? The fine line of voyeurism The boundary between observing and spying is fragile. It does not necessarily lie in physical distance, nor even in the act of photographing someone without their knowledge. It may lie in the intention behind the gaze. Observing a scene that unfolds naturally in a public space is not the same as deliberately seeking out what ought to remain hidden. Stalking a vulnerability, waiting for a moment of humiliation, isolating a person in a moment of weakness because that weakness would make for a ‘good photograph’: that is when something shifts. The photographer is no longer simply looking. He is taking. And I cannot always resolve this distinction whilst I am out walking. The doubt remains. It sometimes accompanies the moment the shutter clicks. The secret that does not belong to the photographer Photographing someone in a public space does not mean that everything they reveal belongs to the photographer’s gaze. A person in distress. Suffering that is all too evident. An intimacy which, even when exposed in the middle of the street, seems to demand respect. There are situations that can be photographed. And others in which one must know when to put the camera down. This restraint is also part of the photographer’s vision. Perhaps even more so than the ability to produce a beautiful image. A successful photograph does not excuse everything. The photographer does not own what they see. They pass through a world that existed before them and will continue to exist after they have gone.

The Passers-by There is something in Georges Brassens’s ‘Les Passantes’ that moves me deeply: this way of observing people glimpsed for a few moments without ever claiming to know them. Women encountered by chance. Possibilities that will never be realised. Encounters that could have become something but amount to nothing. The street captured in a photograph sometimes looks like this. A succession of lives glimpsed in passing. Faces we shall never know. Lives about which we shall know nothing. A man walks by. A woman crosses the street. Two figures walk side by side, then each goes their separate way. The photographer can capture nothing but their passing. He knows neither their story nor their destination. He possesses only a fragment. And perhaps we should simply accept this ignorance, rather than fabricating a story around them that exists only in our own eyes. That is also what I like about Brassens: his characters remain human beings, with their frailties, their contradictions, their little quirks. They are not reduced to what an outside observer might wish to make of them. Do not embellish. Do not judge. Do not possess. Simply observe.

The mirror of passers-by A street photograph often says as much about the observer as it does about the observed. I might photograph a man sitting alone on a bench. But what am I actually photographing? His loneliness? My idea of loneliness? The light on his face? Or my own desire to make sense of what I do not know? Perhaps this is where voyeurism becomes an interesting photographic question. Because it is not just about what the photographer does to his subject. It is also about what he projects onto him. We look at someone for a few seconds and are tempted to invent a whole life for them. Photography freezes the body. The imagination, however, carries on. The photographer believes they are looking at others. But others also reflect their own gaze back at them.

Being there To photograph the street, you have to be present. Walking without a specific plan. Letting yourself be guided by a light, a silhouette, an almost insignificant situation. But being present does not mean placing yourself above those you are observing. You must be willing to share their space. The same pavement. The same light. The same sound of traffic. Photographing up close, at eye level, also means accepting that you will be seen. That changes things. The photographer is no longer completely hidden behind their camera. They embrace their presence more fully. They, too, become a passer-by amongst the others.

Anticipation Sometimes, the frame is there before the subject. Light cuts across a wall. A shadow crosses the pavement. Architecture forms a geometric pattern. So I wait. Perhaps a human presence will come along to complete what is already there. I don’t know who it will be. I don’t know when. I don’t even know if they’ll come. But something tells me to stay. A passer-by appears. For a fraction of a second, the silhouette, the light and the background seem to come together. Then it all unravels. The scene vanishes. The street resumes its flow. This way of waiting strikes me as important, precisely because it distances the photographer from the hunt for a subject. I’m not chasing anyone. I’m waiting for a situation to arise. The cat’s stance Sometimes you have to photograph the way a cat observes: without haste, without a sound, attentive to the slightest movement. Don’t chase after the scene. Let it come to you. This approach requires a kind of intuition: sensing that a situation may be unfolding even before you know what image it will yield. The gaze then precedes the shutter release. Technique enables you to take photographs. Intuition sometimes tells you when to take a photograph. But it also demands restraint: knowing when not to press the shutter.

The frame and the distance I remain committed to this simple idea: try to compose the shot before pressing the shutter. Look at the lines, the spaces, the bodies, the light, the voids and the shadows. Seek accuracy rather than perfection. The frame becomes a window onto what is about to happen. Over time, I have also become more wary of distance. A long focal length allows you to remain invisible. It allows you to look without being looked at. This is precisely what can make its use unsettling. Being hidden behind a long focal length makes it tempting to become a spectator of the world rather than a participant. Nowadays, I prefer to be more within the scene. Up close. At eye level. Accepting being seen. This closeness does not eliminate voyeurism. But it makes the illusion of invisibility more difficult to maintain.

Black and white Black and white is a natural accompaniment to this way of looking. It strips the world of certain details to bring others into sharper focus. Light becomes more intense. A shadow takes up more space. A face almost disappears into the background. A silhouette becomes a shape. Reality loses some of its precision and perhaps gains in mystery. And that element of mystery strikes me as important. For I do not know who the person I am photographing really is. I do not know what they are thinking. I do not know what they are going through. The image cannot answer these questions. It shows only a single moment.

What we do not see Ultimately, a street photograph shows only a part of what exists. Before the image, there was a step. After the image, the person carried on. We do not know where they were going, what they were thinking, what lay ahead for them. Everything that gives depth to a life remains outside the frame. Perhaps it is better that way. Photography sometimes becomes more accurate when it accepts that it cannot know everything. It suggests. It leaves room for the unknown. It does not necessarily turn a passer-by into a story. It simply preserves their trace.

The strangers on the street This way of looking accompanies me as I walk through Paris. I am drawn to ordinary silhouettes – those who do not seek to be noticed, those who pass by the capital’s expected images. It is not the monuments that interest me most. It is the people who live around them. Those who wait, work, are bored, love, walk, or seem lost in thought. The city then becomes less a backdrop than a multitude of parallel lives. And perhaps this is where voyeurism takes on a different character. I no longer seek to intrude on someone’s life. I am content merely to catch a glimpse of its surface. For just a moment. Just as each of us does every day whilst walking down the street.

Doubt After taking a photograph, a question sometimes remains: why this image? An attitude? A light? An emotion? Or simply the pleasure of having caught a glimpse of something that wasn’t meant for me? I don’t always have the answer. And perhaps it’s better not to have it. Doubt is perhaps the only safeguard against the certainty of having the right to photograph anything and everything. It forces me to return to the original question: am I looking, or am I spying? The answer isn’t always comfortable. Perhaps it shouldn’t be.

The mirror Deep down, photographing passers-by is perhaps akin to photographing our own way of looking at the world. What I choose to photograph says something about me. So does what I decide not to photograph. In this silent relationship between the observer and the passer-by, there is something that resembles a mirror. The passer-by carries on their way. The photographer stays for a few seconds. He takes the shot. Then each goes their separate ways. The photograph remains as a tiny trace of an encounter which, without it, might never have existed. And perhaps that is what photographing the street is all about, after all: approaching without possessing, looking without spying, capturing without stealing. The person passes by. The light changes. The shadow disappears. The street carries on.
